Retailers feel pressure to clear out old stock in order to make room for new stock.

They have to have a certain amount of product turn-over to be profitable. If they buy an item at wholesale, and it fails to sell at retail, they reduce the price in order to get it out the door and make room for a new item that is more appealing for purchase.

I agree that there was a lot of double-talk in that interview. I once knew a lawyer and any time I would ask him a question (related to legal matters or not) he would always inhale deeply, pause to collect his thoughts, and then habitually answer in a way that used the most multi-syllabic words possible to say as little as possible. I came to suspect that that's pretty much what 90% of the training and education for business and contract law involved: teaching people to use a lot of words to say essentially nothing.

One thing that does make sense from those interviews, however, is the practice of discounting physical copies of games in order to help retailers get rid of excess stock. No business owner wants to have money tied up in product that isn't going to move because nobody wants to pay the asking price anymore. And retailers of packaged games aren't exactly thriving these days.

When you get right down to it, games sold in physical form are not going to be around for much longer. Half the time, all people are getting in the box is a few pamphlets, a skimpy instruction manual, and a disc with a launcher/updater on it. The environmental cost alone (when compared to digital distribution) is reason enough to stop producing games in physical packages. The only thing stopping physical distribution altogether is that developers know they still have millions of dollars in annual income to be earned from people in remote areas who have poor/no reliable internet to manage multi-GB downloads.

Greed, I think, is a word that gets tossed around inappropriately sometimes. I don't know the inner workings of Ubisoft's financial situation, but I know that gamers have certainly haven't gradually come to expect less of developers, that's for sure. More features, higher audio and visual fidelity, better voice-overs, better story, better support, better polish at launch...these things don't happen for free.

Ubisoft's higher-ups would have been better off just using plain English. People would accuse them of lying because some people assume everything is a lie, and people would accuse them of greed because some people assume all profitable businesses are greedy, but at least they couldn't be accused of being cryptic and not forthcoming with their response.
